stories.headline: NHL Tonight: What to watch in Bruins-Red Wings, Canadiens-Devils, Avalanche-Mammoth
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
It's another relatively light schedule of NHL games Wednesday night, with just three showdowns on the docket.

But one completes the Original Six series that began Monday, another pits two of the East's top contenders, and the third is a preview for the upcoming Winter Classic. Not too shabby!

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Boston Bruins at Detroit Red Wings

7:30 p.m. ET (TNT) | DET -122, O/U: 6.5

Monday was Rangers-Canadiens, Tuesday was Blackhawks-Maple Leafs, and thus we finish the Original Six series this week with Bruins-Red Wings.

Boston has been at or near the top of the Atlantic Division standings this season, while Detroit has been at or near the bottom. This is the first of four games between the teams this season; they'll square off again Dec. 5, Jan. 9 and Feb. 27.

In the post-Dylan Larkin era -- or at least non-Dylan Larkin era -- Lucas Raymond (21 points) and Alex DeBrincat (16) have been shouldering the scoring load. Boston has been led by newly minted captain David Pastrnak (26 points), with Elias Lindholm finding an old scoring gear as well (17).

The B's have an advantage overall in both goals per game (3.55 to 2.62) as well as goals allowed per game (2.60 to 2.95).

The backup tenders for each team (Michael DiPietro and Daniil Tarasov) have better marks in goals-against average and save percentage than the starters (Jeremy Swayman and John Gibson), so it'll be intriguing to see who gets the nod in each crease.

Montreal Canadiens at New Jersey Devils

7:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NJ -162, O/U: 6.5

Each of these clubs has played 21 games this season, and the Devils are two points ahead in the standings; those 30 points are good enough for second place in the Metro, while the Canadiens' 28 has them third in the Atlantic.

Connor Hellebuyck has started his Devils career with a perfect 7-0-0 record, and has gone 13-7-2 in his career against the Canadiens, with a 2.89 GAA and .909 SV%. On the other side, the Habs have a decision to make between super rookie Jacob Fowler -- who has been generally superb, but had a rough go on Monday -- or Jakub Dobes, who was incredible in the 2026 playoffs but not quite so incredible so far this season.

The Devils' biggest strength so far has been their scoring punch, ranking second in the East in goals. Center Jack Hughes (10 goals, 17 assists) is leading the way, followed by his current linemates Jesper Bratt (four goals, 17 assists) and Arseny Gritsyuk (eight goals, nine assists).

Meanwhile, the Canadiens are paced in scoring by defenseman Lane Hutson (three goals, 16 assists), right wing Cole Caufield (12 goals, seven assists) and center Nick Suzuki (eight goals, nine assists).

Colorado Avalanche at Utah Mammoth

10 p.m. ET (TNT) | UTA -108, O/U: 6.5

Both teams made the playoffs last season, and on some nights each of them look every bit the part of a legit Stanley Cup contender.

There have been some off nights too, however, which has each team's playoff spot anything but secure right now in the always-competitive Central Division.

As with the B's and Wings, one of these teams has an edge both in goals for and against this season; it's the Avalanche, who are scoring 4.05 and allowing 3.00 per contest, while the Mammoth are at 3.32 and 3.46, respectively.

Colorado will again be without superstars Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar, who are out with long-term injuries. Nick Schmaltz and Dylan Guenther are among the injured players for Utah.

After this showdown, the two teams play again on Dec. 14, and their next matchup will be held at Rice-Eccles Stadium (home of the University of Utah football team).

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.

stories.headline: Man United to take legal action if JJ Gabriel was illegally approached - sources
stories.summary: Manchester United are prepared to mount legal action if they find evidence that JJ Gabriel has been illegally approached by other clubs while under contract, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
Manchester United are prepared to mount legal action if they find evidence that JJ Gabriel has been illegally approached by other clubs while under contract, sources have told ESPN.

Gabriel announced his departure from Old Trafford with a video posted on social media on Tuesday. Sources have told ESPN that United were unaware of the announcement until it was published.

United still hold Gabriel's registration and sources have told ESPN there has been no contact with any governing body about transferring the 16-year-old's registration to another club.

A verbal agreement is in place for Gabriel to sign for Real Madrid. He can join a club within the European Union as a domestic or EU player, bypassing non-EU foreign player quotas, because he has an EU passport.

Real Madrid were approached for comment by ESPN but have not yet responded.

The teenager has not been back to Carrington since walking out in September.

Sources have told ESPN that United staff have made a number of attempts to check on Gabriel's welfare, but have not been able to make contact with his family.

United, according to sources, believe Gabriel's family and representatives may have held meetings with rival clubs as early as last summer.

Gabriel refused a request from United to train with the academy at the start of preseason before joining the first-team squad on a full time basis. A number of demands were also made by his representatives ahead of the season.

They included Gabriel playing at least 20 minutes in first-team games against Sabah FK, Brighton and Bournemouth, for the forward to be assigned the No.77 squad number and to have the name "Gabriel JR" on his shirt.

stories.headline: Kayla Harrison, Amanda Nunes reclaim leading roles in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Who do Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes replace in ESPN's P4P women's top 10?
stories.body:
Hello (again), Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes. Goodbye (for now), Valentina Shevchenko and Zhang Weili. The top of the ESPN women's MMA pound-for-pound rankings has a new look.

Harrison and Nunes, both of whom had been ineligible for the top 10 because of inactivity, returned over the weekend for a clash of elites at UFC 334. Harrison, defending her bantamweight championship for the first time after nearly a year and a half out of the cage while healing from surgery for herniated discs in her neck, scored a fourth-round submission of Nunes, who had been retired for nearly 3½ years. As a result, Harrison takes over the No. 1 ranking and Nunes, a former two-division champion and the consensus GOAT of women's MMA, is No. 2.

The former occupants of those spots, Shevchenko and Zhang, are newly ineligible for the rankings because it's been over a year since they have fought and they have nothing scheduled. Those two former champions drop out, and the rest of the women's top 10 remains the same.

In the men's rankings, UFC heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane moves up one spot to No. 7 on the strength of his decision win over Josh Hokit in their title bout at UFC 334.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Nov. 18. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Kayla Harrison

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 20-1

Last: W (Sub4) vs. Amanda Nunes, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Harrison stepped into the Octagon at UFC 334 already a reigning champion, but her submission win over Nunes was truly her crowning achievement. The backstory about their shared training gym history added drama to the buildup, but what mattered most about this matchup was that Harrison, who had voiced her goal to be the greatest ever in women's MMA, was facing the woman who has lived up to that standard. After choking out Nunes, what can Harrison do for an encore? Can any other woman in the sport give her a fight? Maybe it won't come to that. Harrison and Nunes both called for a rematch -- but at featherweight. That would lessen Harrison's burden in dealing with her toughest foe: the weigh-in scale.

2. Amanda Nunes

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 23-6

Last: L (Sub4) vs. Kayla Harrison, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Nunes' return from retirement did not go as she had hoped, but her failing was not so much about deteriorated physical abilities as it was about her ill-advised choice to venture too much into Harrison's grappling wheelhouse. If Nunes gets the rematch both women are calling for, but at 145 pounds, that would seem to be to the advantage of Harrison, the bigger woman. But a redo would give Nunes the opportunity to lean into her own strength as a striker.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 13-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Virna Jandiroba, Nov. 7

Next: TBA

If Suarez was still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Loopy Godínez. Then she went on to beat another fellow top-10 strawweight, Jandiroba, sending a message to the division that Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

8. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

9. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

10. Jasmine Jasudavicius

UFC flyweight

Record: 16-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Erin Blanchfield, Oct. 17

Next: TBA

Jasudavicius was rising in the 125-pound division until being knocked out by Manon Fiorot last year, halting a five-fight winning streak. But she got back up and won two in a row, most recently an impressive grappling performance against Blanchfield, to reassert herself as a contender.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Virna Jandiroba.

How our panel voted

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Harrison; 2. Cyborg; 3. Silva; 4. Nunes; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Jasmine Jasudavicius.

Andrew Davis: 1. Harrison; 2. Nunes; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Fiorot; 9. Suarez; 10. Jasudavicius.

Dre Waters: 1. Harrison; 2. Cyborg; 3. Nunes; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Joselyne Edwards.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Harrison; 2. Nunes; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Suarez; 9. Ditcheva; 10. Jasudavicius.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 15-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Josh Hokit, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ made his first defense against Hokit at UFC 334, winning a slugfest.

8. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

9. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.

Other fighters receiving votes: Alexandre Pantoja and Sean Strickland.

How our panel voted

stories.headline: Passan: 2026-27 MLB offseason preview, free agent updates
stories.summary: The hot stove is about to get blazing hot. Here's what will shape the coming weeks of offseason moves.
stories.body:
The rush is coming. It's likely to start with pitchers and eventually wind its way to position players. There will be a few trades, none particularly league-shaking. Money will be spent. Everything will look relatively normal, actually. And then Major League Baseball, whose offseasons usually toil on endlessly, postseason bleeding into hot stove spilling into spring training, will just stop.

When the league locks out the players as the clock turns from Dec. 1 to Dec. 2, the sport will shut down entirely, transactions grinding to a halt, which separates free agents into two groups: pre-lockout and post-lockout. Conversations at the GM meetings last week offered the first sliver of clarity as to how those groups will sort themselves. Tuesday's qualifying-offer deadline and the rash of players designated for assignment are other data points worth considering. How teams act when this week's owners meeting end will further solidify just how wild the 10 days leading up to the lockout will be.

The first two weeks of free agency have delivered three deals of moderate significance and two of interest: first baseman Jake Bauers getting $58 million over four years from Boston, Dustin May's surprise three-year, $52.5 million contract with the Chicago White Sox and reliever Evan Phillips booking $35 million from Atlanta for three seasons. Closer David Bednar returning to the Yankees and catcher Ryan Jeffers doing the same for the $23.15 million qualifying offer took two more interesting pieces off the board. Now, all the attention turns to the best player in the class, who is certainly in the pre-lockout signing cohort --- and his own category.

Tarik Skubal
Skubal met with the New York Mets on Monday and the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays on Tuesday. He is expected to round out his in-person get-togethers with the San Diego Padres this week. By the time he signs -- and it could be sooner than later -- it will be the largest deal for a pitcher in baseball history. For a player like Skubal, even the teams that want a salary cap are willing to break the bank.

The Mets left their meeting with Skubal impressed, reinforcing their status as favorites. But to call this a one-team race simply does not reflect the reality of Skubal's market. Yes, Toronto playing winter bridesmaid is a well-worn meme after failed pursuits of Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Kyle Tucker. In Skubal's case, do not discount the Blue Jays. They are flush with cash and prepared to spend it, hoping to pair the two-time Cy Young winner with Dylan Cease for a truly nasty top of the rotation. Players love the city and the organization, and that sort of reputation only bolsters the Blue Jays' case.

As for the rivals in Southern California, new San Diego owner Jose Feliciano recognizes the need to keep the Padres competitive and is willing to spend to do so. Will he guarantee upward of $400 million, with three contracts of $280 million or more on the books already? That ... sounds like something the Dodgers might do. And while they're typically the favorite in these situations, the Dodgers are playing it cool right now. Maybe it's sandbagging. Maybe their austerity, or a desire to deal in shorter-term contracts, is real. We'll know only when the bids start coming in -- and that could be imminently.

The busiest teams
After following up a 2025 World Series appearance with a last-place finish in the AL East, the Blue Jays are exploring every avenue to improve. Adding the slugging Brandon Lowe at second base? Sure. He's going to get a big number from someone, though, and if it's not him heading to Toronto, maybe it will be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is garnering interest across MLB because of his production, versatility and willingness to sign a shorter-term, prove-it type contract. And if it's not either of them, it could be Teruaki Sato or Seiya Suzuki -- the former coming from Japan to great fanfare and the latter the most sought-after MLB free agent on the hitting side. It could be two of them, too. At this point in the offseason, nothing is off-limits for the Blue Jays.

The Padres aren't talking with quite as many players, but their presence with Skubal suggests a level of seriousness with which few other organizations operate. Four years after missing out on Suzuki when he signed with the Cubs, the Padres hosted him for a visit Monday and could be the favorites to add him, allowing Fernando Tatis Jr. to return full time to the infield. The actual level of resources Feliciano commits is one of the more intriguing stories considering he paid nearly $4 billion for the Padres -- signifying the sort of rise in franchise value that MLB hopes to achieve with a salary cap.

The Baltimore Orioles are everywhere. Depending on how the next two weeks go, they could find themselves on the verge of carrying a top-10 payroll. The Orioles are not hesitating to dip their toe in any pool. Bats and arms. Free agency and trades. Just about everyone on their roster is available. They'll move players from their infield glut for a controllable arm. They'll give the right free agent starter three years-plus. (They were in the neighborhood on May.) Urgency has arrived.

And don't look now, but the Colorado Rockies -- whose owner, Dick Monfort, is front and center among owners when it comes to labor issues -- are talking like they're going to spend this winter after their fourth consecutive season of 100-plus losses. While plenty of money will go to infrastructure, an area in which the Rockies have found themselves woefully behind, they're also hopeful that some brave starting pitchers will agree to multiyear contracts at the sort of price that compensates them properly for the peril of starting half of their games at Coors Field.

The guaranteed signings
With the acknowledgement that nothing is guaranteed until the ink dries on a term sheet, nobody has more incentive to sign in the coming weeks than the three top Japanese players who want to join MLB next season: infielder/outfielder Teruaki Sato and right-handers Kaima Taira and Hiromi Itoh. Though all three typically would have a 45-day window to sign, MLB will not pause the posting system -- which allows foreign players to join a team -- and reopen it post-lockout. Which means if any of the three want to join MLB next season, they need to be signed before Dec. 2.

Sato is the best bat available in the class, ranking No. 2 in Kiley McDaniel's free agent rankings, and has been the object of serious affection -- perhaps none greater than the Philadelphia Phillies' interest. He will do the best of the trio and could be signed before Thanksgiving. As for the others ...

So many starters
The most interesting lane of the market right now is starting pitching because nobody is quite sure what the order of operations looks like -- and who that might leave without a chair when the music stops. May glided into the first chair Tuesday, perhaps signaling the start of more action.

The way the last lockout-impacted offseason played out, the best pitchers (Kevin Gausman and Robbie Ray) waited until just before the lockout to sign. The veteran equivalents this time around: Michael King and Freddy Peralta, who will land two of the biggest deals -- both pre-lockout -- this winter. After that, things are less certain.

Do teams looking for a longer-term solution jump on Trevor Rogers, the youngest domestic starter in the class, early? The list of teams that need pitching is lengthy. It includes the Cubs, Mets, Giants, Rockies, A's, Royals, White Sox (even after landing May), Reds, Guardians and Marlins. And the reality is, every one of them could sign a quality big league starter between now and Dec. 2.

Right-handed veterans abound. Sonny Gray, Nick Martinez, Gausman and Matthew Boyd fit perfectly in any rotation -- and are expected to command two years tops, satisfying the teams looking for shorter-term options.

Want to lock a guy up for the long term? Joining May in the three-year club could be Clay Holmes, Foster Griffin, Tyler Mahle and Michael Soroka, who, at 29, has youth and a 4-to-1 strikeout-to-walk ratio on his side. While not all of them will get that sort of deal, the patient ones will happily join the post-lockout side in hopes that desperation for pitching will supersede the effect of any incoming economic system.

Two left-handers who won't need to wait: Kris Bubic and Patrick Sandoval, both of whom, despite histories littered with injuries, have boards more than a dozen deep with teams that want to hand them a rotation spot today.

Other starters could float to post-lockout if they don't choose to jump the market to go into winter with a job: Jack Flaherty, Shota Imanaga, Casey Mize, Zac Gallen, Shane Bieber, David Peterson. Nick Pivetta will likely wait out the lockout and could find himself in a far more advantageous position months down the road, particularly if he can spend the downtime healing an arm that prompted San Diego to decline a $14 million option.

Not many relievers
Yankees closer David Bednar accepting the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer illustrated how the market for high-paid relief pitchers can be very tricky. No long-term deal materialized. The Yankees weren't going to bid against themselves. And so Bednar will carry the highest single-season salary ever for a closer into 2027.

Adrian Morejon turned down the QO, confident that his market will make it worthwhile. There are no other free agents in his echelon, and the one closer with similar performance to Morejon's who was thought to be available via trade, Trevor Megill, could stay with the Brewers for now before a post-lockout decision. The only other free agent closer, Raisel Iglesias, wants $20 million and will probably settle for about 80% of that whether it's pre- or post-lockout.

A few other relief pitchers should do well -- and sign before the deadline. Jonathan Loaisiga will get multiple years as a setup man or closer. Bryan Abreu, coming off a dreadful first half, righted himself enough to get multiple years. A.J. Minter's consistency will carry him. Like his ex-teammate Phillips, left-hander Alex Vesia is shooting for three years and could get it.

With a glut of mid-tier relievers, prices could stagnate and force some very difficult decisions for players: Take a deal that seems below-market now for security's sake or come out jobless after an untold number of months into an uncertain market that could be governed by an unfamiliar system.

The remaining bats
The biggest name not to sign before the lockout could be outfielder Randy Arozarena. He has suitors, yes, but they are balking at his ask of well over $100 million, and with the abbreviated time before the lockout, compromise can be difficult to come by. This doesn't mean Arozarena won't sign. Losing out on another player or two can prompt a team to amend its offer -- or just go on tilt. But unless something changes, he could be the Freddie Freeman of this class, ready to cash in once the lockout lifts.

There is one even bigger name potentially available: Texas shortstop Corey Seager, whom the Rangers are open to moving. The issue: Seager is not as open, and with a full no-trade clause, he wields the power to spike any deal, as do Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi, both of whom likewise are covered by no-trade protection. Seager has indicated an openness to moving, but it's to fewer than a handful of teams, and there is no current momentum on a deal. Certainly that will be revisited leading up to Dec. 1 -- and this could also be a classic post-lockout blockbuster.

There could be some lockout deadline-beating trades involving hitters in the meantime. Kansas City and San Francisco, both desperate to upgrade their rotations, have floated infielders Maikel Garcia and Casey Schmitt for pitching help.

On the free agency front, Mauricio Dubon, like Garcia a Gold Glove winner, can play anywhere and is a popular target. The only player this winter with more Gold Gloves than his three is outfielder Ian Happ with four, and between his glove, power potential and ability to draw walks, he is drawing a wide variety of interest and will have his pick of pre- or post-lockout.

Alec Bohm is a pre, with more than a half-dozen teams showing interest and giving him a suite of one- and two-year options. Between him and Ty France, anyone seeking a first-base solution now has options. Center fielder Tyrone Taylor is similarly a favorite among teams and has positioned himself to get well above the public expectation pre-lockout, while other regular center fielders (Daulton Varsho, Luis Robert Jr., Trent Grisham) might be post-lockout types.

Perhaps the most interesting case of the bunch is among the biggest names: Luis Arraez, the three-time batting champion who's hopeful his second foray into free agency goes better than his first. Do the ball-in-play abilities of the teams that made it to both league championship series this year help Arraez, the foremost contact artist in MLB? Or are teams that were scared to offer him a multiyear deal at 28 last winter still hesitant despite another three-win season in which Arraez played better defense and remained the best sort of nuisance at the plate?

We'll know the answer in two weeks when baseball goes away, its comeback not guaranteed, its momentum stopped cold, the game forced into hibernation by a fight that will only get worse before it gets better.

stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: Las Vegas Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 is back under the bright lights of Las Vegas for one of the most extravagant weekends on the calendar.
stories.body:
Formula 1 is back under the bright lights of Las Vegas for one of the most extravagant weekends on the calendar.

Lando Norris clinched his third victory this season at the São Paulo Grand Prix after new world champion Kimi Antonelli spun out of the lead in wet conditions.

Max Verstappen had a masterful drive in his Red Bull and charged his way through the field from 21st to second.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 21st round.

- Qatar, Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as F1 rules out Imola backup plan for finale

- Wet weather mastery by Norris, Verstappen makes Brazil F1's must-see race

- Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad to continue at Racing Bulls for 2027

Las Vegas Grand Prix schedule
All times in GMT

Friday, November 20

Practice One: 00.30 a.m. - 1.30 a.m.

Practice Two: 4 a.m. - 5 a.m.

Saturday, November 21

Final Practice: 00.30 a.m. - 1.30 a.m.

Qualifying: 4 a.m. - 5 a.m.

Sunday, November 22

Las Vegas Grand Prix: 4 a.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Las Vegas Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Las Vegas Strip Circuit
Las Vegas' race is certainly one of the most newest and flashiest street races with one of the most famous backdrops in the world after it took a spot on the F1 calendar in 2023, costing around $500 million.

The street circuit is one of few night races on the calendar, and includes the city's famous Strip and different landmarks around the city, such as the Bellagio and the Sphere.

The best place to watch the action unfold is from a casino, or West Harmon Zone grandstands. Casinos offer high-end packages to watch in specially built race zones around the circuit, but the grandstands around the final corner and viewing the pit straight still offer a great view.

Las Vegas Grand Prix

Circuit: Las Vegas Strip Circuit; Las Vegas, Nevada

Previous winners in Las Vegas

2023: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024: George Russell (Mercedes)

2025: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2023

Laps: 50 laps of 4km

Lap record: 1:33.365, Max Verstappen (2023)

Most wins: Verstappen has the most wins with two (2023 and 2025) and George Russell has one.

Most poles: Charles Leclerc (2023), Russell (2024) and Norris (2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the Las Vegas Grand Prix is cold with temperatures between 10-14°C.

What happened last time out?

McLaren's Norris continued his impressive form in the business end of the season and put in a blistering lap to take pole position.

But come Sunday's race he ran wide at the first corner in an attempt to hold off Red Bull's Verstappen, who took advantage from second to gain the lead.

The Dutchman controlled the lead from that point onwards to win the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Norris and Oscar Piastri ended up being disqualified from the race for a technical infringement -- a major blow in the title race with only two races to go at the time.

Who will win this year?

Mercedes completed the double and wrapped up the constructors' championship last time out, a week after Antonelli was crowned world champion.

With it being a night race, the conditions in Las Vegas are always very cold, a world away from some of the soaring temperatures the drivers race in throughout the year.

McLaren has been running a heavily-upgraded car that seems to be working well, and Norris will be carrying his winning momentum to Vegas.

Verstappen is in strong form and has made his way to second in the title standings with three victories under his belt and 12 podiums this year.

Having won twice in Vegas already, the Dutchman will certainly be the one to watch.
